{{short description|Algorithm for solving a puzzle or game in the fewest possible moves}}
'''God's algorithm of the Rubik cube''' is a notion originating in discussions of ways to solve the [[Rubik's Cube]] puzzle,<ref>Paul Anthony Jones, ''Jedburgh Justice and Kentish Fire: The Origins of English in Ten Phrases and Expressions'', Hachette UK, 2014 {{ISBN|1472116224}}.</ref> but which can also be applied to other [[combinatorial]] [[puzzle]]s and [[mathematical game]]s.<ref>See e.g. ''Rubik's Cubic Compendium'' by Ernö Rubik, Tamás Varga, Gerzson Kéri, György Marx, and Tamás Vekerdy (1987, Oxford University Press, {{ISBN|0-19-853202-4}}), p. 207: "...the Pyraminx is much simpler than the Magic Cube... Nicholas Hammond has shown that God's Algorithm is at most 21 moves (including the four trivial vertex moves). [More recently, three people have found God's Algorithm. The maximal number of moves is 15 (including the four vertex moves).]"</ref> It refers to any algorithm which produces a solution having the fewest possible moves (i.e., the solver should not require any ''more'' than this number). The allusion to the deity is based on the notion that an [[omniscient]] being would know an optimal step from any given configuration.

== Scope ==

=== Definition ===

The notion applies to [[puzzle]]s that can assume a [[wiktionary:Finite|finite]] number of "configurations", with a relatively small, well-defined arsenal of "moves" that may be applicable to configurations and then lead to a new configuration. Solving the puzzle means to reach a designated "final configuration", a singular configuration, or one of a collection of configurations. To solve the puzzle a sequence of moves is applied, starting from some arbitrary initial configuration.

=== Solution ===

An algorithm can be considered to solve such a puzzle if it takes as input an arbitrary initial configuration and produces as output a sequence of moves leading to a final configuration (''if'' the puzzle is solvable from that initial configuration, otherwise it signals the impossibility of a solution). A solution is optimal if the sequence of moves is as short as possible. The highest value of this, among all initial configurations, is known as '''God's number''',<ref>{{cite news |author=Jonathan Fildes  |publisher=[[BBC News]] |title=Rubik's Cube quest for speedy solution comes to an end |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-10929159 |date=August 11, 2010}}</ref> or, more formally, the '''minimax''' value.<ref name=Sing311/> God's algorithm, then, for a given puzzle, is an algorithm that solves the puzzle and produces only optimal solutions.

Some writers, such as David Joyner, consider that for an algorithm to be properly referred to as "God's algorithm", it should also be ''practical'', meaning that the algorithm does not require extraordinary amounts of memory or time.  For example, using a giant [[lookup table]] indexed by initial configurations would allow solutions to be found very quickly, but would require an extraordinary amount of memory.<ref>Joyner, page 149</ref>

Instead of asking for a full solution, one can equivalently ask for a single move from an initial but not final configuration, where the move is the first of some optimal solution. An algorithm for the single-move version of the problem can be turned into an algorithm for the original problem by [[Mathematical induction|invoking it repeatedly]] while applying each move reported to the present configuration, until a final one is reached; conversely, any algorithm for the original problem can be turned into an algorithm for the single-move version by truncating its output to its first move.

== Examples ==

Well-known puzzles fitting this description are [[mechanical puzzle]]s such as [[Rubik's Cube]], the [[Tower of Hanoi]], and the [[15 Puzzle|15 puzzle]]. The one-person game of [[peg solitaire]] is also covered, as well as many [[logic puzzle]]s, such as the [[missionaries and cannibals problem]]. These have in common that they can be [[Mathematical model|modeled mathematically]] as a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)#Directed graph|directed graph]], in which the configurations are the vertices, and the moves are the arcs.

=== Mechanical puzzles ===

==== ''n''-Puzzles ====

The [[Fifteen puzzle]] can be solved in 80 single-tile moves<ref>A. Brüngger, A. Marzetta, K. Fukuda and J. Nievergelt, [http://www.iro.umontreal.ca/~gendron/Pisa/References/BB/Brungger99.pdf The parallel search bench ZRAM and its applications], ''Annals of Operations Research'' '''90''' (1999), pp. 45–63.</ref> or 43 multi-tile moves<ref>{{cite web |last1= Norskog |first1= Bruce |last2= Davidson |first2= Morley |title= The Fifteen Puzzle can be solved in 43 ''moves'' |website= Domain of the Cube Forum |date= December 8, 2010 |accessdate= March 15, 2022 |url= http://cubezzz.duckdns.org/drupal/?q=node/view/223}}</ref> in the worst case. For its generalization the ''n''-puzzle, the problem of finding an optimal solution is [[NP-hard]],<ref>Daniel Ratner, [[Manfred K. Warmuth]] (1986). [http://www.aaai.org/Papers/AAAI/1986/AAAI86-027.pdf "Finding a shortest solution for the N × N extension of the 15-puzzle is intractable"]. in ''Proceedings AAAI-86''. National Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 1986. pp.&nbsp;168–172.</ref> so it is not known whether there is a practical God's algorithm.

==== Towers of Hanoi ====

For the [[Towers of Hanoi]] puzzle, a God's algorithm is known for any given number of disks. The number of moves increases exponentially with the number of disks {{nobr|(<math>2^n-1</math>)}}.<ref>{{cite web |last= Rueda |first= Carlos |title= An optimal solution to the Towers of Hanoi Puzzle |website= Universidad Autónoma de Manizales [Autonomous University of Manizales] |location= [[Manizales]], [[Colombia]] |date= August 2000 |accessdate= March 15, 2022 |url= http://yupana.autonoma.edu.co/publicaciones/yupana/003/hanoi/hanoi_eng.html |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20040605074124/http://yupana.autonoma.edu.co/publicaciones/yupana/003/hanoi/hanoi_eng.html |archive-date= 2004-06-05}}</ref>

==== Rubik's Cube ====
{{main|Optimal solutions for Rubik's Cube}}
[[File:2021-01-14 18 25 51 A scrambled Rubik's Cube in the Franklin Farm section of Oak Hill, Fairfax County, Virginia.jpg|thumb|A scrambled Rubik's Cube]]
An algorithm to determine the minimum number of moves to solve Rubik's Cube was published in 1997 by [[Richard E. Korf]].<ref name=":1">[[Richard E. Korf]], "[https://www.aaai.org/Papers/AAAI/1997/AAAI97-109.pdf Finding optimal solutions to Rubik's Cube using pattern databases]", ''Proc. Natl. Conf. on Artificial Intelligence'' (AAAI-97), Providence, Rhode Island, Jul 1997, pp. 700–705.</ref> While it had been known since 1995 that 20 was a lower bound on the number of moves for the solution in the worst case, Tom Rokicki proved in 2010 that no configuration requires more than 20 moves.<ref name="GN20">{{cite web |last1= Rokicki |first1= Tomas |last2= Kociemba |first2= Herbert |last3= Davidson |first3= Morley |last4= Dethridge |first4= John |title= God's Number is 20 |year= 2010 |accessdate= March 15, 2022 |website= Cube20.org |url= http://www.cube20.org/}}</ref> Thus, 20 is a [[Mathematical jargon#sharp|sharp]] [[upper bound]] on the length of optimal solutions. Mathematician [[David Singmaster]] had "rashly conjectured" this number to be 20 in 1980.<ref name=Sing311>Singmaster, p. 311, 1980</ref>

== Unsolved games ==
Some well known games with a very limited set of simple well-defined rules and moves have nevertheless never had their God's algorithm for a winning strategy determined.  Examples are the board games [[chess]] and [[go (game)|Go]].<ref>Rothenberg, p. 11</ref>  Both these games have a rapidly increasing number of positions with each move.  The total number of all possible positions, approximately {{val|5|e=44}}<ref>{{cite web |url=https://github.com/tromp/ChessPositionRanking |title=Chess Position Ranking |website=[[GitHub]] |author=John Tromp}}</ref> for chess and 10<sup>180</sup> (on a 19×19 board) for Go,<ref>Baum, p. 199</ref> is much too large to allow a brute force solution with current computing technology (compare the now solved, with great difficulty, Rubik's Cube at only about {{val|4.3|e=19}} positions<ref>Singmaster, 1981</ref>).  Consequently, a brute force determination of God's algorithm for these games is not possible.  While chess computers have been built that are capable of beating even the best human players, they do not calculate the game all the way to the end.  [[Deep Blue (chess computer)|Deep Blue]], for instance, searched only 11 moves ahead (counting a move by each player as two moves), reducing the search space to only 10<sup>17</sup>.<ref>Baum, p. 188</ref>  After this, it assessed each position for advantage according to rules derived from human play and experience.

Even this strategy is not possible with Go.  Besides having hugely more positions to evaluate, no one so far has successfully constructed a set of simple rules for evaluating the strength of a Go position as has been done for chess, though neural networks trained through reinforcement learning can provide evaluations of a position that exceed human ability.<ref>{{multiref|Baum, p. 197|Mohammadian, p. 11}}</ref>  Evaluation algorithms are prone to make elementary mistakes<ref>Baum, p.197</ref> so even for a limited look ahead with the goal limited to finding the strongest interim position, a God's algorithm has not been possible for Go.

On the other hand, [[draughts]] (checkers) has long been suspected of being "played out" by its expert practitioners.<ref>Fraser & Hannah, p. 197</ref>  In 2007 Schaeffer ''et al.'' proved this to be so by calculating a database of all positions with ten or fewer pieces, providing a God's algorithm for all end games of draughts which was used to prove that all perfectly played games of draughts end in a draw.<ref>Moore & Mertens, chapter 1.3, "Playing chess with God"</ref>  However, draughts with only {{val|5|e=20}} positions<ref>Schaeffer ''et al.'', p. 1518</ref> and even fewer, {{val|3.9|e=13}}, in the database,<ref>Moore & Mertens, "Notes" to chapter 1</ref> is a much easier problem to solve – of the same order as Rubik's cube.

The magnitude of the set of positions of a puzzle does not entirely determine whether a God's algorithm is possible.  The already solved Tower of Hanoi puzzle can have an arbitrary number of pieces, and the number of positions increases exponentially as <math>3^n</math>.  Nevertheless, the solution algorithm is applicable to any size problem, with a running time scaling as <math>2^n</math>.<ref>Rueda</ref>
